access.onlyHidden: only hidden in Hata — the port stays open
access.others: Other ports stay open. Tick the ones that serve web pages to require sign-in there too:

access.how: With sign-in required, Hata listens on the app's port itself and lets in only people who are signed in to Hata and allowed to open the app; the address stays the same. Without it, a restriction only hides the app in Hata. Administrators can always open everything. Only the app's web port is protected: other ports stay open unless ticked, and only ports that serve web pages can be protected. An app on another computer then opens through this server, on a port of this server, and no longer at the computer's own address. The app also receives who opened it in the headers Remote-User, Remote-Groups (admins, users or guests) and X-WebAuth-User, so an app that supports proxy authentication needs no sign-in of its own. Apps on the host network cannot be protected — their ports stay open.

import.lead: Containers on this server that are not Hata apps yet. Once imported, they get a tile, updates, backups and sign-in like any other app.

import.projectsHint: Started with docker compose somewhere else
import.source.file: Hata copies this compose file and manages the same containers from now on. Nothing is restarted; the original file stays where it is and is no longer used.
import.source.resolved: The project's file depends on its location (relative paths, its own variables), so Hata saves it fully resolved, as compose reads it now. Nothing is restarted; the original files stay where they are.
import.source.containers: The project's compose file was not found on this server, so this one is generated from its running containers. They keep running as they are and are recreated from this file at the next start or update, with the same volumes.
import.containerLead: This compose file is generated from the container's settings. Check it and change what you need — it becomes the app's file.
import.step.stop: Container {name} is stopped and kept under another name.
import.step.start: The app is started from this file, with the same folders and volumes — no data is copied or deleted.
import.step.remove: When the app is running, the old container is removed.
import.step.undo: If the app does not start, the old container is restored as it was.
import.warn.links: The container uses --link to reach another container. Compose has no equivalent: put both on one network, or the link is lost.
import.warn.volumesFrom: The container takes volumes from another container (--volumes-from). They are written here as its own volumes; check the list.
import.warn.sharedNetwork: The container shares the network of another container. This is not in the file: add network_mode: "service:…" or "container:…" by hand.

notify.push.title: Devices
notify.push.lead: A notification from the browser or from Hata installed as an app, on this phone or computer. Each administrator turns it on for their own devices.
notify.pushNeedsHttps: Browsers allow notifications only on a page opened over HTTPS. Set a domain in Network → Addresses and HTTPS, open Hata by it — and this device can be switched on here. Telegram, ntfy, mail and a webhook work without it.
notify.pushUnsupported: This browser cannot receive notifications. On an iPhone or iPad, add Hata to the home screen first (Share → Add to Home Screen) and open it from there.
notify.denied: Notifications are blocked for this page in the browser — allow them in the site's settings and try again.
notify.pushFailed: The browser could not subscribe to notifications: {message}
notify.telegram.title: Telegram
notify.telegram.lead: Messages from a bot of your own: create one with @BotFather, paste its token here, and write anything to the bot from the chat that should get the messages.
notify.telegram.chatHint: The number of the chat, or @name of a channel. "Find" lists the chats that wrote to the bot lately.
notify.telegram.noChats: Nobody has written to this bot lately. Send it any message and press "Find" again.
notify.ntfy.title: ntfy
notify.ntfy.lead: A topic on ntfy.sh or on an ntfy server of your own; the ntfy app on the phone shows what arrives.
notify.ntfy.urlHint: The server and the topic, like https://ntfy.sh/my-topic. Whoever knows the topic's name can read it — pick one that cannot be guessed.
notify.webhook.title: Webhook
notify.webhook.lead: A POST request with JSON (title, text, severity, code, app, url, server, time) to an address of yours — for n8n, Home Assistant, a script.
notify.email.title: E-mail
notify.email.lead: An e-mail sent through an SMTP server — your mail provider's (for Gmail, Outlook or iCloud with an app password, not the account's own) or a relay of your own.
notify.email.hostHint: The SMTP server and its port, as the provider names them.
notify.email.securityHint: STARTTLS on 587 or TLS on 465 — whichever the provider says. Without encryption the password is sent over the network in plain text: only for a server in your home network.
notify.email.userHint: Usually the whole address. Leave empty for a server that needs no sign-in.
notify.email.passwordHint: For Gmail, Outlook and iCloud — an app password made in the account's security settings.
notify.email.fromHint: The sender's address; most providers require the one you sign in with.
notify.email.toHint: One address or several, separated by commas.
error.notify.badMailHost: The server's name does not look like a host name or an address.
error.notify.badMailPort: The port is a number from 1 to 65535.
error.notify.badMailAddress: One of the addresses does not look like an e-mail address (or there are more than ten).
error.notify.badMailUser: The user name or the password contains a line break.
error.notify.needMail: To send e-mail, fill in the server, From and To.
notify.test.title: Test message from Hata
error.notify.bad: These notification settings cannot be saved.
error.notify.badToken: This does not look like a bot token: it is a number, a colon and a long string.
error.notify.badChat: The chat is a number (it can start with a minus) or @name of a channel.
error.notify.needTelegram: Telegram needs both the bot token and the chat.
error.notify.badNtfy: The topic address has to be a web address ending in the topic's name, like https://ntfy.sh/my-topic.
error.notify.badUrl: The address has to start with http:// or https://.
error.notify.badSubscription: The browser's notification subscription is not one Hata can use.
error.notify.tooManyDevices: Too many devices are subscribed — remove the ones no longer used.
error.notify.telegramRefused: Telegram did not accept this token (or the bot is set to deliver its updates to a webhook).
edit.lead: The app's compose file as a form. What the form does not show stays in the file as it is; comments in the file are not kept. The Compose tab has the whole file.
edit.broken: The compose file of this app cannot be read as YAML — fix it on the Compose tab.
edit.title: Title
edit.webUiHint: Where the tile leads when Hata is opened by its address: the address, the port and the path. Leave the address empty for this server and the port empty for an app without a page.
edit.webDomainHint: The app's own address when Hata is opened by its domain: {names}. Hata forwards it to the port above. Leave it empty to use the app's name.
edit.webDomainElsewhere: Not used while the address above names another computer: the tile leads there.
edit.volumesHint: A folder of the server (an absolute path) or the name of a Docker volume, and where the container sees it.
edit.rawHint: Written in a way the form has no fields for; it is kept as it is unless you remove it. Change it on the Compose tab.
edit.privilegedHint: Gives the container nearly everything the server itself may do.
store.custom.formLead: Describe the container; Hata writes the compose file.
store.custom.fileLead: Paste a compose file. It is saved as is and started with `docker compose`.
store.custom.runLead: Paste the command from the app's instructions. The form is filled in from it for you to check and install — nothing is started before that.
error.edit.invalid: The form could not be saved as sent — reload the page and try again.
error.edit.badImage: Enter the Docker image, like nginx:alpine.
error.edit.badPort: A port is a number from 1 to 65535; the container's port is required.
error.edit.badVolume: A volume needs a folder of the server (an absolute path) or a volume name, and an absolute path in the container.
error.edit.badEnv: A variable needs a name made of letters, digits and underscores.
error.edit.sameEnv: The same variable is listed twice.
error.edit.badDevice: A device is a path on the server, like /dev/ttyUSB0, and a path in the container.
error.edit.badCapability: Capabilities are names like NET_ADMIN, separated by commas.
error.edit.badIcon: The icon has to be a web address starting with http:// or https://.
error.edit.badWeb: The address on the home network is a host name, a port from 1 to 65535 and a path.
error.edit.badDomain: The name under the domain is one word of Latin letters, digits and hyphens, up to 63 characters.
error.edit.domainTaken: The app {app} already uses this name. Choose another one.
error.edit.badService: A service needs a name of its own made of letters, digits, - and _, and an app needs at least one service.
run.ignored: These options have no field in the form and were left out — add them on the Compose tab afterwards if the app needs them:
error.run.notRun: This is not a docker run command.
edit.removeServiceLead: The service and everything set for it is removed from the form. Its container is stopped and removed once the form is saved; its folders and volumes stay.
edit.iconHint: The address of a picture, or a picture of your own: PNG, JPEG, WebP, AVIF or SVG, up to 1 MB.
edit.iconOwn: Your own picture is used; it is kept next to the app's compose file as icon.*. Remove it to go back to the address.
error.icon.tooLarge: The picture is too large: {max} MB at most.
error.icon.notImage: This is not a picture Hata can show: PNG, JPEG, WebP, AVIF or SVG.
state.title: Configuration folder
state.lead: Where Hata keeps its settings, Home, and each app's compose file and icon. Users, passwords and keys are kept separately, in /etc/hata, and are not moved with it. App data is not here — it is in the data folder above.
state.folderHint: To move it, enter another folder — a new or an empty one — and press Move. Everything is copied there and Hata restarts; the apps keep running.
state.notMovable: It can be moved from here only when Hata runs as the installed service.
state.moveLead: Everything in {from} is copied to {to} and Hata restarts from there — the page comes back in a few seconds. The apps keep running. The old folder is not deleted: it is renamed and left where it was.
state.inDataRoot: This is inside the data folder ({path}). An app that is given the whole data folder would also see Hata's settings and every app's compose file, with any passwords in it — choose a place apps do not reach if you can.
state.moving: Moving the configuration folder — Hata is restarting…
state.notBack: Hata has not come back yet. Reload the page in a moment; if it still does not open, check the service's log on the server.
error.state.badPath: Enter an absolute path to a folder of your own — not the root and not a system folder.
error.state.nested: The new folder cannot be inside the current one, or hold it.
error.state.notEmpty: That folder is not empty. Choose a new one or an empty one.
error.state.busy: Something is being installed or changed right now — wait until it is done.
error.state.copyFailed: The folder could not be copied: {message}
error.state.notService: The configuration folder can be moved only when Hata runs as the installed service.
offsite.title: A second copy somewhere else
offsite.enableHint: The backups here stay as they are; this is a second copy, in case this server is lost.
offsite.pathHint: Without a leading slash it starts at the user's home folder.
offsite.keyHint: Add this line to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys of {user} on the other computer. Hata signs in with this key, never with a password.
offsite.sealHint: Files are encrypted before they leave: whoever keeps them cannot read them.
offsite.passphraseKept: saved — leave empty to keep it
offsite.passphraseHint: Write it down somewhere else. Without it the copy cannot be opened — restoring on a new computer asks for it. A new passphrase applies only to snapshots sent from then on.
offsite.denied: The other computer refused the sign-in: add Hata's key above to authorized_keys of that user, then save again.
offsite.noSftp: This server has no sftp. Install the package openssh-client.
offsite.inStep: In sync with this server · checked {when}
offsite.hostLead: Hata is connecting to this computer for the first time. Its key:
offsite.hostHint: To be sure it is the same computer, compare the key with the output of this command on it:
error.offsite.badHost: The address must be a host name or an IP address.
error.offsite.badPort: The port must be a number from 1 to 65535.
error.offsite.badUser: The user name may contain letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores.
error.offsite.badPath: The folder must not be empty or contain quotes, backslashes, *, ?, brackets or "..".
error.offsite.badPassphrase: The passphrase must be at least 8 characters.
attention.offsite.title: The second copy of the backups is out of date
activity.system.offsite.failed: Sending the second copy of the backups failed
disks.title: Disks
disks.lead: Each disk's own health data (SMART), read every half an hour. Sleeping disks are not woken for it.
disks.limits.title: When to warn
disks.limits.lead: Reallocated or unreadable sectors and a failed self-test are always reported. The rest is yours to set below.
disks.limits.hotHdd: Warn about a hard disk's temperature from
disks.limits.hotHddHint: From 30 to 90 °C. Hard disks wear faster above about 55 °C; their makers usually allow up to 60.
disks.limits.hotFlash: Warn about an SSD or NVMe disk's temperature from
disks.limits.hotFlashHint: From 30 to 110 °C. NVMe disks run warm and slow themselves down at about 70–80 °C.
disks.limits.wear: Warn about an SSD's wear from
disks.limits.wearHint: From 10 to 100% of the drive's rated write endurance, as the disk itself counts it.
disks.none: No disks are visible from here. Inside a container Hata sees only the file systems it was given.
disks.tool.missingHint: SMART is read with smartctl from the smartmontools package, which is not installed on this server. On Debian and Ubuntu the package also turns on its own service, smartd; Hata does not need it, and it can be turned off with systemctl disable --now smartd.
disks.tool.denied: Hata has no access to the disks
disks.tool.deniedHint: Reading SMART needs root on the computer itself; in a container the disks are usually out of reach.
disks.fs.title: File systems
disks.fs.lead: Where files are kept on this server, connected drives included.
disks.noSmart: This disk reports no SMART data: a virtual disk, or a USB enclosure that hides it.
disks.finding.failing: The disk itself reports that it is failing. Copy what matters off it now and replace it.
disks.finding.critical: The drive reports a critical fault. Copy what matters off it now and replace it.
disks.finding.spare: The drive is running out of spare blocks: {n}% left. Replace it.
disks.finding.test: The last self-test failed. Copy what matters off the disk and replace it.
disks.finding.reallocated: The disk has moved {n} damaged sectors to its spare area. It still works, but disks that start doing this fail more often — keep a second copy of what is stored only here.
disks.finding.pending: {n} sectors could not be read and wait to be moved. Keep a second copy and plan a replacement.
disks.finding.uncorrectable: {n} sectors hold data the disk could not recover. Keep a second copy and plan a replacement.
disks.finding.media: The drive could not read data {n} times (media errors). Keep a second copy and plan a replacement.
disks.finding.worn: The drive has used {n}% of the writes it is rated for. Plan a replacement.
disks.finding.hot: The disk is hot: {n} °C. Heat shortens its life — check the airflow around it.
disks.value.reallocatedHint: damaged and moved to the spare area
disks.value.uncorrectableHint: data the disk could not recover
disks.value.mediaHint: data the drive could not read
disks.value.crcHint: a cable or a port, not the disk itself
disks.value.wearHint: of the writes the drive is rated for
disks.test.hint: The disk tests itself and stays usable meanwhile: a short test takes about two minutes, a long one reads the whole surface and takes hours.
fills.title: What fills {path}
fills.lead: The data folder measured once a day: its folders, each app's data and the trash. Growth is the change over the last week.
fills.never: Not measured yet. Hata measures the folder once a day in the background; for a large folder the first time takes a few minutes.
fills.outsideHint: the system, Docker's images and everything else on this disk
mounting.title: Using this disk
mounting.formatHint: Erases the disk and makes a new file system on it.
mounting.absent: the disk is not connected now
mounting.foundHolds: It holds: {what}. Hata has not changed anything on it.
mounting.foundEmpty: It looks empty. Hata has not changed anything on it.
mounting.mergeLead: The disks ticked below show up as one folder that is as large as all of them together. A new file goes to the disk with the most free room; every file stays a plain file on one of the disks, readable there without Hata.
mounting.mergeWarn: This adds room, not safety: there is no second copy, and a disk that fails takes the files that were on it. The disks stay connected on their own too, and the merged folder waits for all of them at start.
mounting.needs.mergerfs.what: What is missing: mergerfs, a small system package that shows several folders as one.
mounting.needs.mergerfs.why: What for: it is what puts the disks together; the files themselves stay ordinary files on each disk.
error.disk.badMerge: Choose at least two folders that Hata connected and that are in no merged folder yet.
error.disk.noMergeTool: The program that merges disks is not installed.
error.disk.holds.pool: This disk is part of a merged folder. Disconnect the merged folder first.
mounting.blocked.system: The system runs from this disk, so Hata will never erase it.
mounting.blocked.mounted: A part of this disk is connected by something other than Hata, so the whole disk cannot be formatted.
mounting.blocked.swap: The disk is in use as swap space.
mounting.blocked.member: The disk is part of an array, a volume group or an encrypted volume. Hata does not touch those.
mounting.formatErases: Everything on this disk will be erased, for good. It holds:
mounting.formatEmpty: The disk looks empty. Whatever is on it will be erased, for good.
mounting.formatPartErases: Everything on this partition will be erased, for good. The other partitions of the disk are not touched.
mounting.formatLeaves: It is connected as {paths} now and will be disconnected first.
mounting.fs.ext4: ext4 — for a permanent disk of this server
mounting.fs.exfat: exFAT — for a disk or a stick used with other devices
mounting.fsHint.ext4: Keeps owners and permissions of files, which apps need for their data. Windows and macOS do not read it.
mounting.fsHint.exfat: Windows, macOS, Linux, phones and televisions of today read and write it; files of any size. No owners or permissions.
mounting.fsHint.vfat: Read by nearly everything, old car stereos, printers and cameras included. No file larger than 4 GB, no disk over 2 TB.
mounting.fsHint.ntfs: The file system of Windows. macOS only reads it; televisions and phones often do not open it.
mounting.label: Label
mounting.labelHint.ext4: The name other devices show the disk under. Up to 16 Latin or 8 Cyrillic letters; may be left empty.
mounting.labelHint.exfat: The name other devices show the disk under. Up to 11 characters, in any language.
mounting.labelHint.vfat: The name other devices show the disk under. Up to 11 capital Latin letters and digits.
mounting.labelHint.ntfs: The name other devices show the disk under. Up to 32 characters, in any language.
mounting.after.keep: Connect it and keep it connected
mounting.after.once: Connect it until it is unplugged
mounting.afterHint.keep: Written to /etc/fstab: the disk is there after every restart, and the server still starts when the disk is not.
mounting.afterHint.once: It shows up as a folder right away, to copy files to; eject it here before unplugging.
mounting.afterHint.no: Nothing is connected: the disk can be unplugged as soon as this is done.
mounting.sizeHint: Leave it empty for one partition over the whole disk ({max}). A smaller one leaves room for another partition, which can be created later from “Details”.
mounting.sizeHintRest: {rest} stay unallocated, for another partition that can be created later from “Details”.
mounting.sizeHintFree: Leave it empty to take all the free room ({max}).
mounting.sizeBad: A size is a number of gigabytes: at least 0.07 and no more than {max}.
mounting.newPartLead: The partition is created in the unallocated space ({free}). Nothing on the disk is erased: the existing partitions stay as they are.
mounting.wipeLead: The disk is left empty, without partitions or a file system — as it came from the shop. To use it again, format it.
mounting.wipeThorough: Overwrite everything, so that nothing can be recovered
mounting.wipeThoroughHint: For a disk you are giving away. Every block is overwritten with zeros: hours for a large disk. Without this only the partition table and file systems are removed, and recovery software can still find the files.
mounting.wipeThoroughFlash: For a disk you are giving away. Every block is overwritten with zeros; an SSD or a stick may keep a few spare blocks this does not reach. Without this only the partition table and file systems are removed, and recovery software can still find the files.
mounting.name: Name
mounting.nameHint: Latin letters, digits, dots, hyphens and underscores.
mounting.typeName: To confirm, type the disk's short name: {name}
mounting.passwordHint: Your Hata password: erasing a disk cannot be undone.
fsck.title: Check {name}
fsck.lead: Checks the file system for damage, such as that left by unplugging a disk without ejecting it or by a power cut. The check itself changes nothing; what it finds can be repaired afterwards.
fsck.leadMounted: The folder {path} is disconnected during the check and connected again afterwards. Stop whatever is using it first.
fsck.ntfs: Only Windows (chkdsk) checks NTFS in full. Here common damage is found and repaired, and the “dirty” flag that keeps the disk from connecting is cleared.
fsck.running: Checking… A large disk takes a long time.
fsck.verdict.fixed: Repaired. Files that lost their folder, if there were any, are now at the top of the disk (in “lost+found” on ext4).
fsck.verdict.errors: Damage found. Nothing has been changed yet.
fsck.verdict.failed: The check could not be finished — see the program's output.
fsck.back: The folder could not be connected again: {message}
relabel.title: Rename {name}
relabel.lead: The label is the name other devices show the disk under. The files are not touched, and the folder it is connected as stays the same.
relabel.leadMounted: The folder {path} is disconnected for a moment and connected again. Stop whatever is using it first.
mounting.readyLead: It is connected as {path}. Apps reach it by that path, and it can be shared over the network like any folder.
data.moveLead: Everything in {from} — the apps' data, media, backups kept there — is copied to the new folder, the apps are pointed at it, and so are the shared folders and the folders on Home.
data.targetHint: A new or an empty folder, usually on a disk you have just connected.
data.moveWarn: The apps are stopped while the files are copied and started again afterwards; a large folder takes a long time. The old folder is not deleted: it stays where it was, with “.moved” and the date added to its name, for you to delete once everything works.
data.chooseTitle: Where to keep the data folder
error.data.badPath: Give an absolute path to a folder of your own — not the root, not a folder of the system and not Hata's configuration.
error.data.samePath: The data folder is already there.
error.data.nested: The new folder cannot be inside the current one, or hold it.
error.data.notEmpty: That folder is not empty. Choose a new one or an empty one.
error.data.busy: Something is being installed or changed right now — wait until it is done.
error.data.isRoot: The data folder is the whole file system (/), which cannot be moved. Type the new folder in the field and save instead.
error.data.hasMounts: Another disk is connected inside the data folder: {paths}. Its files would be left behind — disconnect it or connect it elsewhere first.
error.data.noSpace: There is not enough free space in the new place for everything in the data folder.
error.data.ownerless: The file system of that disk ({fstype}) keeps no owners or permissions for files, and apps need them for their data. Format the disk as ext4 in Storage → Disks (that erases it) or choose another one.
mounting.connectLead: The files on it stay as they are: nothing is erased or changed. They show up as the folder below.
mounting.noOwners: The {fs} file system keeps no owners or permissions: everything on it will be open for reading and writing to every app and every account of the server.
mounting.keep: Connect it again after a restart
mounting.keepHint: Written to /etc/fstab. Without this the disk stays connected until it is unplugged or the server restarts.
mounting.disconnectLead: The files stay on the disk. The folder disappears from the server and is no longer connected after a restart. What uses it is listed below.
mounting.ejectLead: Hata finishes writing, disconnects the folder and switches the disk off. After that it is safe to unplug.
mounting.ejected: {path} is ejected. The disk can be unplugged.
mounting.automountHint: A USB disk with files on it shows up as /mnt/usb-<its label> a few seconds after it is plugged in, for reading and writing. Nothing on it is changed; eject it here before unplugging.
mounting.needs.ntfs-3g.what: What is missing: ntfs-3g, a small system package that reads and writes NTFS, the file system of Windows.
mounting.needs.ntfs-3g.why: What for: it creates, checks and labels NTFS file systems, and opens them where this system's kernel cannot do it by itself.
mounting.needs.fdisk.what: What is missing: fdisk, a small system package with the sfdisk program, which writes a disk's partition table.
mounting.needs.fdisk.why: What for: a disk formatted whole gets a new partition table.
mounting.needs.sfdisk.what: What is missing: sfdisk, a small program that writes a disk's partition table.
mounting.needs.sfdisk.why: What for: a disk formatted whole gets a new partition table.
mounting.needs.util-linux.what: What is missing: util-linux, the system package with the sfdisk program, which writes a disk's partition table.
mounting.needs.util-linux.why: What for: a disk formatted whole gets a new partition table.
mounting.needs.e2fsprogs.what: What is missing: e2fsprogs, the system package that creates ext4 file systems.
mounting.needs.e2fsprogs.why: What for: it creates, checks and labels ext4 file systems.
mounting.needs.dosfstools.what: What is missing: dosfstools, a small system package that creates, checks and labels FAT file systems.
mounting.needs.dosfstools.why: What for: FAT32 is the file system old devices can read.
mounting.needs.exfatprogs.what: What is missing: exfatprogs, a small system package that creates, checks and labels exFAT file systems.
mounting.needs.exfatprogs.why: What for: exFAT is the usual file system of USB sticks and portable disks.
mounting.needs.byHand: Hata does not know this system's package manager: install the {package} package yourself and try again.
activity.system.disk.label: Disk renamed: {target}
error.disk.badName: A name is up to 32 Latin letters, digits, dots, hyphens and underscores, and starts with a letter or a digit.
error.disk.changed: The disks have changed since this window was opened. Close it and look again.
error.disk.inUse: The disk is in use and cannot be changed.
error.disk.folderTaken: There is already a folder with this name under /mnt that is in use or not empty. Pick another name.
error.disk.noPartitionTool: The program that writes partition tables is not installed.
error.disk.noFormatTool: The program that creates this file system is not installed.
error.disk.formatFailed: The disk could not be formatted. {message}
error.disk.badFs: Hata does not work with this file system.
error.disk.tooBigForFat: FAT32 cannot be larger than 2 TB. Choose exFAT.
error.disk.noCheckTool: The program that checks this file system is not installed.
error.disk.noLabelTool: The program that sets this file system's label is not installed.
error.disk.badLabel: This label holds only characters the file system does not support. Type another one.
error.disk.labelFailed: The disk could not be renamed. {message}
error.disk.working: Another long operation — a copy, a move, a format or a check — is still running. Wait until it is done.
error.disk.noRoom: There is no unallocated space on this disk for another partition.
error.disk.badSize: The size does not fit: at least 64 MB and no more than the free space available.
error.disk.wipeFailed: The disk could not be erased. {message}
error.disk.noExfat: This system cannot open exFAT: its kernel has no driver for it.
error.disk.mountFailed: The disk could not be connected. {message} If it was unplugged without ejecting, check it: “Details”, then “Check”.
error.disk.notOurs: This folder was not connected by Hata, so Hata cannot disconnect it.
error.disk.busy: Something is still using the folder. Stop the apps that keep files there and try again. {message}
error.disk.holds.data: The data folder lies on this disk. Move it in Apps → Options first.
error.disk.holds.backups: The backups are kept on this disk. Choose another folder in Backups first.
error.disk.holds.state: Hata's own configuration lies on this disk.
error.disk.holds.share: There is a shared folder on this disk. Stop sharing it first.
error.disk.packageFailed: The package could not be installed. {message}
error.settings.badStorage: The storage settings are not valid.
error.settings.badSmart: Enter a whole number within the range shown under the field.
error.disk.noSmart: This disk does not report SMART data, so a self-test cannot be run.
error.disk.testFailed: The disk refused to start the self-test.
attention.smart.failing.title: Disk {disk} reports that it is failing
attention.smart.failing.text: Copy what matters off it now and replace it.
attention.smart.critical.title: Disk {disk} reports a critical fault
attention.smart.critical.text: Copy what matters off it now and replace it.
attention.smart.spare.title: Disk {disk} is running out of spare blocks
attention.smart.test.title: Disk {disk} failed its self-test
attention.smart.test.text: Copy what matters off it and replace it.
attention.smart.reallocated.title: Disk {disk} is wearing out
attention.smart.reallocated.text: It has moved {n} damaged sectors to its spare area. Keep a second copy of what is stored only there.
attention.smart.pending.title: Disk {disk} has sectors it cannot read
attention.smart.pending.text: {n} sectors are waiting to be reallocated. Keep a second copy and plan a replacement.
attention.smart.uncorrectable.title: Disk {disk} has lost data in some sectors
attention.smart.uncorrectable.text: {n} sectors could not be recovered. Keep a second copy and plan a replacement.
attention.smart.media.title: Disk {disk} reports media errors
attention.smart.media.text: Reading or writing data failed {n} times. Keep a second copy and plan a replacement.

attention.smart.worn.text: {n}% of the rated writes are used. Plan a replacement.

attention.smart.hot.text: Heat shortens its life — check the airflow around it.
disks.tool.what: What it is: a small system package with the smartctl program, which reads a disk's health data (SMART).
disks.tool.why: What for: without it Hata shows the disks, but cannot tell a healthy one from one that is wearing out, show their temperature or warn you before a disk fails.
disks.tool.how: What the button does: runs the command below on this server. On Debian and Ubuntu the package also starts its own background service, smartd. Hata installs nothing until you press it.

shares.title: Sharing
shares.lead: Folders of this server that open on a computer or a phone like a disk of their own — in Explorer, Finder or a file manager, without the browser.
shares.none: Nothing is shared yet. Share a folder here, or from its menu in Files.
shares.error: The last change was not applied. {message}

shares.found.both: No address has to be typed where the network is browsed: this server shows up by itself as “{name}” — under “Network” in Explorer on Windows, in the sidebar of Finder and in the Files app of a phone.
shares.found.windows: On Windows no address has to be typed: this server shows up by itself as “{name}” under “Network” in Explorer. Finder and phones find it by themselves only when the name on the home network ends in .local and is on.
shares.found.browse: In Finder and in the Files app of a phone no address has to be typed: this server shows up by itself as “{name}”.

shares.how.phone: Phone: “Connect to Server” in the Files app of an iPhone, or a file manager that knows SMB on Android — with the same address.
shares.tool.what: What it is: the system package that serves folders over SMB, the network protocol of Windows — the one Windows, macOS, Linux, phones and TVs all understand.
shares.tool.why: What for: without it the folders of this server are reached only through the browser. With it they open like a network disk.
shares.tool.how: What the button does: runs the command below on this server. The package starts its own background service, which listens on port 445. From then on Samba is set up by Hata: its configuration is written from these settings, and the one that was there is kept as smb.conf.before-hata.
shares.tool.byHand: Hata does not know this system's package manager: install the samba package yourself, and sharing will show up here.
shares.tool.note: Sharing needs Samba, which is not installed on this server yet.

agents.title: Access keys
agents.lead: An AI agent — Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor or another program that speaks MCP — can manage this server for you: say why an app is down, update it, install a new one. It connects with a key created here instead of your password, and may do only what the key's level allows.
agents.none: No keys yet: only people who sign in have access to this server.
agents.new.lead: One key per agent or computer, so each can be revoked separately.
agents.new.name: Name
agents.new.nameHint: What the agent does is written into the activity log under this name.
agents.level.read.hint: Sees the state of the server, the apps and their logs, backups, disks, the store, the other computers, the containers and VMs of Proxmox and of this server, the network, DNS and ad blocking, domains and ports, shared folders and connected drives, remote access, system updates, Home Assistant's devices, torrents and Frigate's cameras. Changes nothing.
agents.level.operate.hint: Also starts, stops, restarts and updates apps, installs apps from the store and takes snapshots, here and on other computers; wakes computers; starts, shuts down, restarts, snapshots and backs up containers and VMs, of Proxmox and of this server; pauses and resumes torrents; pauses ad blocking and allows or blocks a domain; switches Home Assistant's devices, but never unlocks a door or opens a garage or gate; checks for system updates.
agents.level.full.hint: Also changes compose files, installs apps from a compose file, removes apps, moves them to another computer and restores snapshots; restarts and shuts down computers; stops containers and VMs by force, rolls them back, changes, copies and deletes them and creates new ones, in Proxmox and on this server; changes domain names, ports, DNS records and ad-blocking lists; installs system updates; adds and removes torrents; reads the DNS query log (which domains devices look up) and what the cameras saw. An app can be given the whole server through its compose file — give this level only to an agent you would trust with an administrator's password.
agents.levels.title: The levels
agents.never: No key of any level reaches users and passwords, the keys themselves, files, the terminal, nor the tokens and consoles of Proxmox; none formats disks, changes the server's network or shared folders, or updates or removes Hata itself. Values in compose files that look like secrets (passwords, tokens) are hidden from keys below “Everything”. Logs are shown as they are — and whatever an agent reads is sent to the company whose model it runs on.
agents.remove.title: Remove the key “{name}”?
agents.remove.lead: The agent that uses it loses access at once. This cannot be undone — a new key has to be created and given to the agent.
agents.rename.title: Rename the key “{name}”
agents.rename.lead: The agent keeps working with the same key. What it did before stays in the activity log under the old name.
agents.how.title: How agents connect
agents.how.address: The address of the MCP server (Streamable HTTP). The key goes in the header “Authorization: Bearer <key>”; what to paste into the agent is shown when a key is created.
agents.how.plain: This page is open over plain HTTP: on the way to the server a key can be read by whoever is on the same network. From outside, use the HTTPS address.
agents.made.title: The key “{name}” is ready
agents.made.lead: Copy it now: it is shown only this once, and Hata keeps no copy of it.
agents.made.claudeHint: Run this command on the computer where Claude Code is.
agents.made.desktopHint: Put this into claude_desktop_config.json (Claude Desktop → Settings → Developer → Edit Config) and restart Claude Desktop. It reaches the server through the bridge mcp-remote, which npx downloads — Node.js has to be installed on that computer.
agents.made.configHint: The same as an entry of the agent's MCP settings (the file is usually called mcp.json or .mcp.json).

assistant.title: Assistant
assistant.lead: Ask in your own words — “why is Jellyfin down?”, “what takes up the disk?”, “update everything” — and the assistant checks the server and acts, with the same tools an outside agent has. It reads right away, but shows you every change first: nothing changes until you press “Run”. Hata has no model of its own — choose one below.
assistant.provider.openai: OpenAI-compatible: OpenAI, OpenRouter, Ollama and others
assistant.url.openai: Leave empty for OpenAI's own. A model on your own computer: Ollama is “http://<address>:11434/v1”, LM Studio “http://<address>:1234/v1”. The model must be able to call tools.
assistant.keyHint: Kept on the server next to the other secrets and never shown again. A local model may not need one.
assistant.keySaved: saved — type a new one to replace it
assistant.modelHint: The model's name as the provider calls it. “Show the models” lists what this key may use.
assistant.modelsFound: Models found: {n} — pick one in the field
assistant.level.asks: Every change is shown to you before it runs.
assistant.level.full: Every change is shown to you before it runs. At this level the assistant reads compose files whole, with the passwords in them.
assistant.privacy: What the assistant reads to answer you — the state of the server and the apps, their logs, compose files — is sent to the provider of the model. With a model on your own computer nothing leaves your network. Chats are kept on this server, the latest 30 for each administrator.
assistant.notSet: The assistant is not set up yet.
assistant.notSetHint: It needs a model: an API key from Anthropic or OpenAI, or a model on your own computer.
assistant.canDo: Once set up, the assistant can:

assistant.can.machines: see the other computers, the containers of this server and the Proxmox servers
assistant.can.backups: take and restore snapshots, install and update apps

assistant.waitingQuestion: Your question is saved: it will be in the input field once the assistant is set up.
assistant.helloHint: I see the apps and their logs, the disks, backups, computers, containers, Proxmox, the network, the DNS server and Home Assistant. Every change I show you first.

network.lead: The network interfaces of the server. Changing an address goes through NetworkManager, and every change is checked: unless this page reaches the server again in time, the previous settings come back by themselves.
network.addressHint: With the prefix length after the slash: 192.168.1.10/24.

network.readOnly: Hata only shows this interface: it is managed by a service Hata does not configure.
network.stopped: NetworkManager is installed but not running.

Its SIM, PIN and operator are set up on the modem's own page (http://{gateway}, from the server). A backup connection takes over when the main one goes away — the cable pulled out, the router off; with “Check that the internet works” on, also when the router is on and its internet is down.
error.network.badRole: Choose the main connection, a backup one or none.

activity.network.role.backup: {target} is a backup connection to the internet

hotspot.passwordHint: 8 to 63 Latin letters, digits and symbols.

hotspot.scan: Point a phone's camera at the code to join.

error.network.noAp: This adapter cannot be an access point.
error.network.hotspotOnlyWay: This Wi-Fi network is the server's only connection: as an access point the adapter would disconnect from it, and Hata would become unreachable. Connect a cable first.

wifi.endsHotspot: The adapter cannot be an access point and stay connected to a network at the same time: joining a network turns the access point “{ssid}” off.

network.shareHint: The server acts as a router on this port: a computer or a switch plugged into it gets addresses from the server and reaches the internet through the server's main connection. Use a spare port, not the one you reach the server through.
error.network.shareMain: The internet comes in through this interface, so it cannot be shared through it too.

attention.internet.main.text: {nic} is connected but has no internet, so the internet goes through {other}. It switches back by itself when the internet returns.

attention.internet.none.title: The server has no internet

network.shareAddressHint: With the prefix length: 192.168.50.1/24. Devices plugged in get addresses of the same network. Empty — NetworkManager picks one (10.42.x.1/24).
network.address6Hint: With the prefix length after the slash: 2001:db8::10/64.
network.dns6Hint: Up to three IPv6 addresses. Empty — the ones the router gives.

wifi.otherPasswordHint: Empty — a network without a password.

array.title: RAID with parity (SnapRAID)
array.lead: One disk holds parity for the others (SnapRAID): if any one disk fails, its contents are rebuilt from the rest. The disks stay ordinary disks with ordinary files. The parity is only as current as the last sync — what was added or changed since is not protected yet — so it suits media and backups, not what apps write all day.
array.needs.what: What is missing: snapraid, a small system package that computes and checks the parity.
array.needs.why: What for: this RAID is done by SnapRAID. Installing it changes nothing by itself: nothing runs until you choose the disks.
array.needsDisks: It takes at least two disks that Hata connects again after a restart, with a Linux file system (ext4, xfs, btrfs): one for the parity, one or more with data. The disks found here, and why each is or is not suitable, are listed below.
array.fit.title: Disks on this server
array.fit.dataOnly: suitable for data only (not as the parity disk)
array.fit.system: the system runs from this disk
array.fit.member: part of a RAID array, a volume group or an encrypted volume
array.fit.blank: no file system — format it as ext4 and choose to connect it again after a restart (the format dialog has that choice)
array.fit.foreign: {fs} — SnapRAID needs a Linux file system; format it as ext4 (what it holds is erased)
array.fit.notConnected: not connected — connect it with “Connect it again after a restart” ticked
array.fit.temporary: connected temporarily — disconnect it and connect it again with “Connect it again after a restart” ticked
array.fit.pool: a merged folder — the disks it is made of take part, not the folder
array.fit.byHand: mounted at {path} not by Hata (manually or by its own line in /etc/fstab) — unmount it, remove that line, and connect it here
array.turnedOn: The RAID is set up. Start the first sync when the disks hold what you want protected.

array.parityLostHint: A new disk in place of the parity disk looks like this. Nothing is lost as long as the data disks are intact — the parity is rebuilt from them, which reads every disk in full.
array.errorsHint: A check read data that differs from what was written — a disk is failing, or a file was silently corrupted. The parity can repair it; also check the disks' health in Storage → Disks.
array.held: The sync is paused: {n} files are missing since the last one
array.heldHint: That is more than the limit, and a sync would make the parity forget them. If they were deleted by mistake, they can still be brought back.
array.syncAnyway: They were deleted on purpose — sync
array.how: Choose one disk for the parity, a second one if you like, and the disks to protect. A parity disk must be at least as large as the largest protected one, and must not hold the data folder, the backups or a shared folder.
array.parityDiskHint: Its space is taken by the parity file; keep your own files elsewhere.

array.cannot.holds: the data folder, the backups or a shared folder are on this disk — cannot hold the parity
array.appDataHint: Off by default. Apps write there all day, so much of it would always be newer than the parity, and restored files lose their owners — which breaks databases. AppData is covered by the backups.
array.limit: Pause the sync when more files are missing than

array.scrubHint: Reads an eighth of the data and compares it with what was written, so damage is found while it can still be repaired.
array.anew: With a different set of disks the existing parity is of no use: it is removed, and the first sync computes it from scratch. Until then nothing is protected.
array.offLead: Nothing is synced or checked any more. Your files are not touched.
array.offWipeHint: Without the RAID it only takes up space; but without it, turning the RAID on again starts from scratch.
array.recoverLead: Every file the parity knows on this disk and that is missing now is rebuilt. Files that are there are not touched.
array.recoverHow: For a disk that failed: the new one has to be connected as {disk} — formatted under the same folder name — and the others must be in place. It takes as long as reading all the disks.
array.recoverOwners: The parity does not store owners or permissions: restored files get the owner of the disk's top folder and are readable by everybody.

tools.lead: The system programs Hata uses: what each is for and whether it is installed. Nothing is installed or removed until you press its button; the command is shown.
tools.docker.what: Every app runs in it: an app is a compose file that Docker runs. Without it nothing can be installed or started.
tools.samba.what: Shares folders over SMB with Windows, macOS and phones. Hata manages its whole configuration.
tools.smartmontools.what: Reads a disk's SMART data: its health, wear and temperature.
tools.fdisk.what: Writes a disk's partition table (sfdisk) when a disk is formatted whole.
tools.e2fsprogs.what: Creates, checks and labels ext4 file systems, and prevents writing into the folder of a disconnected disk.
tools.dosfstools.what: Creates, checks and labels FAT32 — the file system old devices read.
tools.exfatprogs.what: Creates, checks and labels exFAT — the file system of USB sticks and portable disks.
tools.ntfs-3g.what: Creates, checks and labels NTFS, the file system of Windows, and reads and writes it on systems whose kernel has no NTFS driver.
tools.mergerfs.what: Shows several disks as one folder; the files stay ordinary files on each disk.
tools.snapraid.what: Computes and checks the parity, so that the contents of a failed disk can be rebuilt from the other disks.
tools.network-manager.what: Changes the server's network: addresses, Wi-Fi, an access point, internet connections. Without it Hata only shows the interfaces.
tools.wpasupplicant.what: Wi-Fi passwords and encryption: NetworkManager joins networks through it.
tools.dnsmasq-base.what: Hands out addresses to devices that join the server's access point or a port that shares the internet.
tools.openssh-client.what: Sends the second copy of the backups to another computer (sftp) and makes Hata's own key for it.
tools.ntfs-3g.builtIn: The kernel of this system reads and writes NTFS by itself (the ntfs3 driver), and Hata connects NTFS disks through it.
tools.removeLead: The program is removed from the system. Its settings and data stay, so after installing it again everything works as before.
tools.removeDocker: Every app stops and stays down until Docker is installed again. The apps' compose files, their data, the images and the volumes are not touched.

tools.holds.shares: The shared folders work through it. To remove it, stop sharing them first.

tools.holds.wifi: The Wi-Fi connection or the access point runs through it. Leave the network or turn the access point off first.

welcome.againHint: The first choices for a new server: its name, what already runs here, the modules, where the data and the backups go, the first apps.
welcome.server.title: Name this server

remote.lead: With Tailscale this server joins your own private network. A phone or a laptop with Tailscale, signed in to the same account, reaches Hata, the apps and the shared folders from anywhere — no port is opened on the router and no public address is needed.
remote.what: What is missing: Tailscale — a program that keeps an encrypted connection (WireGuard) between your devices.
remote.why: What for: to reach this server from outside the home network with no port opened. Tailscale is another company's service: it needs an account there (free for personal use), and that service knows which devices are yours — the traffic between them it cannot read.
remote.how: This is Tailscale's own installer: it adds Tailscale's package repository for this system and installs the program. Nothing is connected until you sign in.
remote.stopped: Tailscale is installed, but its service is not running.

wg.lead: WireGuard is an encrypted tunnel with no third party in between: your devices connect directly to this server, or this server connects to another one.
wg.what: What is missing: the WireGuard tools (wireguard-tools) — the programs that set a tunnel up. WireGuard itself is part of the Linux kernel.
wg.why: What for: Hata writes the tunnel's configuration, and these programs bring the tunnel up and show who is connected.

outside.title: {nic} — the outside network (WAN)
outside.lead: For an interface the internet comes in on: a provider's cable plugged straight into the server, or a network of strangers. On it the server closes:
outside.what.pages: Hata's pages and the apps — Docker's published ports included;
outside.what.announce: the server's name on the network (.local) and in Windows' “Network”.
outside.what.remote: Tailscale and WireGuard also stop offering that network to your devices as the home one.
outside.still: The server still reaches the internet through it, and an access point or a port sharing the internet keeps working. Still let in: replies to the server's own requests, IPv6 service messages, the ports of WireGuard (while it is on) and Tailscale, ports opened for the outside network in Network → Addresses and HTTPS, and port 53 while a wildcard certificate is confirmed through Hata's DNS server. The rules are the iptables / ip6tables chain HATA-OUTSIDE.
outside.needs.why: iptables writes the rules that close the outside network. It is the standard Linux firewall tool, which Docker uses too.
outside.exposed: This interface has a public address ({address}): anyone on the internet can open Hata's sign-in page, the apps and maybe the shared folders through it. If the internet comes in here, mark it as the outside network.

tools.holds.outside: It keeps the interface marked as the outside network closed. Mark it as the home network first.

netplace.none: A folder of a NAS, another computer or a cloud can be mounted here as an ordinary folder — over SMB, NFS, SFTP, WebDAV or FTP — and used from Files, by apps and for backups.
netplace.connectTitle: Connect a drive from the network
netplace.dialogLead: The connection is tested first: if the server refuses it, nothing is saved and the server's error is shown. An app's database on a connected drive can be damaged when the connection drops.
netplace.removeLead: {path} is unmounted and removed from this list. Nothing is deleted on the other computer.
netplace.readOnlyHint: Files on the drive cannot be changed or deleted from this server.

netplace.kind.nfsLead: An exported folder of a NAS or a Linux server.
netplace.kind.sftpLead: A folder of any computer you can reach over SSH.
netplace.kind.webdavLead: A folder of Nextcloud, ownCloud, a NAS or any WebDAV server.
netplace.kind.ftpLead: A folder of an FTP server; with TLS when the server supports it.

netplace.nameHint: The drive's name on this server; its folder under /mnt/net is named after it.
netplace.hostHint: The server's name or IP address, and the port if it is not the standard one.

netplace.tlsHint: The sign-in and the files are encrypted; the server has to support it.

pool.title: RAID
pool.lead: How should the disks be used? Each one stays an ordinary disk with ordinary files, readable without Hata too.
pool.goal.both.what: The data disks appear as one folder, and one more disk holds the parity: if any one disk fails, its contents are rebuilt from the others. The parity is as fresh as the last nightly sync. Needs three disks or more.
pool.goal.merge.what: The disks appear as one folder as large as all of them together (mergerfs). This adds space, not safety: if a disk fails, the files on it are lost.
pool.goal.protect.what: The disks stay separate folders, and one more disk holds the parity (SnapRAID). Good for media and backups, not for data that apps change all day.
pool.arrayOn: The RAID is already set up — change it in Storage → RAID.
pool.disksLead.both: Tick the disks to use, then choose the one that holds the parity — the others are merged.
pool.disksLead.protect: Tick the disks to use, then choose the one that holds the parity — the others are protected.
pool.parityHint: Must be at least as large as the largest of the other disks. Its space is used by the parity file.
pool.inPool: part of a merged folder already
pool.do.format: will be formatted as ext4 — everything on it is erased
pool.do.keep: will be connected permanently instead of temporarily
pool.mergedHint: The folder where the disks appear as one. New files go to the disk with the most free space.

pool.todo.protect: Protect {disks}: the parity on {parity}; sync every night at {time}
pool.erases: Everything on these disks will be erased: {disks}.

pool.done.both: Done: the disks are merged into one folder, {path}, and protected.
pool.done.merge: Done: the disks are merged into one folder, {path}.
pool.syncHint: Nothing is protected until the first sync. Start it now, or it will run by itself tonight; on large disks it takes hours.

pve.addLead: Hata manages Proxmox VE through its API with a token created there: nodes, containers and virtual machines, storages, backups. Nothing is installed on Proxmox, and the token can do only what Proxmox allows it.
pve.urlHint: As in the browser: 192.168.1.10, pve.local:8006 or https://pve.example.com. Without https:// the port is 8006.
pve.tokenHint: user@realm!name, as Proxmox shows it, e.g. hata@pve!panel
pve.secretKeepHint: Leave empty to keep the saved secret.
pve.name: Name
pve.nameHint: The name shown in Hata. Empty: the cluster's name, or the node's.
pve.howTitle: How to create a token in Proxmox
pve.how.1: Datacenter → Permissions → Users → Add: a user such as hata, realm Proxmox VE authentication server (no password is needed).
pve.how.2: Datacenter → Permissions → API Tokens → Add: the user, a token ID such as panel. Copy the secret — Proxmox shows it once.
pve.how.3: Datacenter → Permissions → Add → User Permission and API Token Permission: path /, the role PVEAuditor — to see everything.
pve.how.4: To manage too: the role PVEVMAdmin on the containers and VMs or a pool of them, PVEDatastoreUser on the storages for backups.
pve.howRights: With privilege separation on (the default), the token can do only what both the user and the token are allowed. Hata shows only the actions the token allows.
pve.certTitle: Is this the certificate of your server?
pve.certLead: The server uses a self-signed certificate ({subject}, issued by {issuer}), not one issued by a public authority. Compare the fingerprint:
pve.certWhere: In Proxmox: the node → System → Certificates, pve-ssl.pem, Fingerprint. Once you confirm it, Hata connects to this server only while it presents this certificate.
pve.removeLead: Hata deletes the saved address and token. Nothing changes on Proxmox: delete the token there too if it is no longer needed.
pve.noJobs: No backup jobs are set up in Proxmox.

pve.rebootLead: The system inside is asked to restart; whatever runs there stops for a while.
pve.stopLead: Like pulling the plug: nothing inside gets to save its work. Use it when a normal shutdown does not work.
pve.snapshotLead: Proxmox keeps the disks as they are now, on the same storage; you can roll back to a snapshot in seconds. It is not a backup: if the disk fails, the snapshot is lost with the storage.

pve.rollbackLead: Everything written inside after the snapshot {snapshot} is lost. A running container or VM is stopped for the rollback.
pve.snapshotRemoveLead: The current state does not change; you just can no longer roll back to {snapshot}.

pve.client.title: Hata's client on {name}
pve.client.lead: The client is a small program that runs inside as a service and connects to this Hata by itself — no port has to be opened. The container or VM then becomes one of the computers:
pve.client.gives.apps: store apps and the Docker containers inside are installed, updated and started from here, and shown on Home with the others;
pve.client.gives.files: its files open in Files and can be copied and moved to and from this server;
pve.client.gives.terminal: a terminal inside it and in each of its Docker containers, in the browser;
pve.client.gives.backups: snapshots of its apps are kept here with the others and restored from here;
pve.client.gives.power: its state and system updates, and starting it from Hata when it is off.
pve.client.step1: Open the console in Proxmox (sign in there if asked):
pve.client.step2: Sign in as root and paste this command; it installs curl if needed, downloads the client from this Hata, verifies it and starts it.
pve.client.step3: This window shows when the computer has connected.
pve.client.step3stopped: It is stopped: start it first. This window shows when the computer has connected.

pve.client.autoLead: Hata signs in on the container's console as root with the password you enter here, runs the command and waits for it to finish. The password is used once and not stored.
pve.client.done: Hata's client is installed on {name}; it is now one of the computers

raid.title: Arrays and pools
raid.lead: Arrays and pools this server already has: Linux software RAID (md), ZFS pools, btrfs on several disks. Hata monitors their state, warns when one loses a disk or finds damage, and can start their own check. It does not create or change them.
raid.dataErrors: {n} files damaged and cannot be repaired
raid.needs.zfs: ZFS disks are here, but the ZFS tools are not installed
raid.needs.zfsWhy: Hata needs the zpool program to read a ZFS pool. On Ubuntu the zfsutils-linux package is enough. On Debian ZFS comes with a kernel module built for your kernel, so it is installed by hand: enable the contrib section, then install zfs-dkms and zfsutils-linux.
mounting.needs.btrfs-progs.what: What is missing: btrfs-progs, the system package that makes, checks and names btrfs.
mounting.needs.btrfs-progs.why: What for: without it btrfs cannot be created, and a btrfs pool across several disks cannot be read or checked.
error.raid.unknown: This array or pool no longer exists.
error.raid.badAction: This action is not available for this array or pool.
error.raid.busy: Another operation is already running on it. Wait until it finishes.
error.raid.notWhole: A check runs only on a healthy array. Replace the missing disk first.
error.raid.cannotStop: A rebuild cannot be stopped from Hata: interrupting it would leave the array without redundancy for longer.
error.raid.notMounted: The file system is not mounted, so btrfs cannot run this on it.
attention.raid.failed.title: {pool} has failed: its data cannot be read
attention.raid.failed.text: Too many of its disks are missing or have failed, or it was not assembled at startup. Its data is unavailable until the disks are back: Storage → RAID.
attention.raid.degraded.title: {pool} is degraded: a disk is missing
attention.raid.degraded.text: The data is still intact, but one more disk failure may destroy it. Replace the disk: Storage → RAID shows which one.
attention.raid.rebuilding.title: {pool} is rebuilding a disk: {percent}%
attention.raid.rebuilding.text: Until the rebuild finishes, the data is not protected from another disk failure. Keep the server on.
attention.raid.damaged.title: {pool} has damaged files
attention.raid.damaged.text: {n} files could not be repaired from another copy. Restore them from a backup.
attention.raid.errors.title: The disks of {pool} report errors
attention.raid.errors.text: {n} read, write or checksum errors. A check repairs what it can from another copy. Look at the health of the disks, then reset the counters: Storage → RAID.
attention.raid.mismatch.title: {pool}: the check found mismatches
attention.raid.mismatch.text: The last check found {n} mismatches. Repair them, then check again: Storage → RAID.
mounting.fs.btrfs: btrfs — for a permanent disk, with checksums and snapshots
mounting.fs.xfs: XFS — for a permanent disk with large files
mounting.fsHint.btrfs: Keeps owners and permissions, and a checksum of every block, so corruption is detected instead of going unnoticed. Windows and macOS cannot read it.
mounting.fsHint.xfs: Keeps owners and permissions; fast with large files and with many files. It can be enlarged later, but never shrunk. Windows and macOS cannot read it.
mounting.labelHint.btrfs: The name the disk is shown under. Up to 255 Latin or 127 Cyrillic letters; may be left empty.
mounting.labelHint.xfs: The name the disk is shown under. Up to 12 Latin or 6 Cyrillic letters, without spaces; may be left empty.
mounting.needs.xfsprogs.what: What is missing: xfsprogs, the system package that makes, checks and names XFS.
mounting.needs.xfsprogs.why: What for: it creates the file system; reading XFS needs nothing extra — the kernel does it.
tools.btrfs-progs.what: Makes, checks and names btrfs, and reads and checks btrfs pools across several disks.
tools.xfsprogs.what: Makes, checks, names and enlarges XFS.
tools.holds.btrfs: A btrfs disk is connected, and Hata watches it through these tools. Disconnect it first.
fsck.btrfs: btrfs is only checked here, not repaired. Damage is repaired by a scrub while the disk is connected: it restores a block from its copy when there is one. Repairing a disconnected btrfs is known to make things worse.
fsck.xfs: If XFS was not disconnected cleanly, connect and disconnect it once before the repair, so that its journal is replayed.
error.disk.noRepair: This file system cannot be repaired while disconnected.

resize.lead: The partition can grow into the free space right after it, or shrink; its files stay in place.
resize.leadGrow: The partition can grow into the free space right after it; its files stay in place.
resize.leadShrink: The partition can be shrunk; its files stay in place.

resize.xfs: XFS can be enlarged, but never shrunk.
resize.noRoomAfter: The partition cannot grow: the space right after it is taken. Delete or shrink the next partition first.
resize.offline: {path} is disconnected while it is resized and connected again afterwards. Stop the apps that keep files there first.
resize.backup: Resizing is safe if it runs to the end, but a power cut midway can leave the partition unreadable. Back up what matters first.
resize.passwordHint: Your Hata password: this changes the partition table.
partDelete.title: Delete partition {name}
partDelete.lead: The partition and everything on it will be erased permanently. Its space becomes free for a new partition; the disk's other partitions are not touched.

error.disk.noTable: Hata could not read the disk's partition table.

incus.title: Containers and virtual machines of this server
incus.lead: Separate Linux systems on this server, run by Incus: each can have its own Docker, apps or anything else.
incus.blocked.title: Containers cannot be created here
incus.blocked.nested: Hata itself runs inside an unprivileged container (for example a Proxmox LXC container), which gets only a part of the user IDs. Containers and virtual machines cannot be created inside such a container.
incus.blocked.how: Create them on the host this container runs on (the Proxmox server), or on a computer where Hata is installed directly.
incus.missing.title: Containers need Incus
incus.missing.lead: Incus runs system containers: lightweight separate Linux systems that share this server's kernel. Hata installs it only when you press the button.
incus.gives.system: A whole Linux system, such as Debian, Ubuntu or Fedora, with its own address, packages and users
incus.gives.docker: Docker inside, apart from the Docker of this server
incus.gives.machine: With Hata's client inside, it becomes one of the computers, with its apps, files and terminal
incus.gives.snapshots: Snapshots to roll back to, and CPU and memory limits
incus.missing.what: The packages incus-base (containers, about 110 MB) and dnsmasq-base (addresses on the containers' network) are installed from this system's repository. Hata then creates a storage pool in /var/lib/incus and the network hatabr0.
incus.missing.byHand: Hata installs Incus on Debian and Ubuntu. On this system install it by hand, then come back here.
incus.setup.title: Incus is installed but not set up
incus.setup.lead: Hata creates what is missing: a storage pool, the network hatabr0 with internet access, and the default profile. Existing settings are left as they are.
incus.noneLead: Create one: it gets its own address on the containers' network, and with Hata's client inside it appears among the computers.
incus.newLead: The system is downloaded once from the image server of Incus and kept for the next containers.
incus.name: Name
incus.nameHint: Small letters, digits and dashes; it is also the host name.
incus.imageHint: Only systems tested with Hata are offered.
incus.clientHint: The container becomes one of the computers: its apps, files, terminal and backups in Hata.
incus.dockerHint: Installed with Docker's official script; nesting is turned on for the container.
incus.bad.name: The name: small letters, digits and dashes, starting with a letter, up to 63.
incus.bad.image: Choose a system from the list.
incus.bad.snapshot: A snapshot's name: letters, digits, dots, dashes, underscores.
incus.made.machine: {name} is ready and connected to Hata
incus.col.name: Name
incus.consoleHint: A root shell inside this system.
incus.screenHint: The virtual machine's screen; your keyboard and mouse control it.
incus.limitsLead: Applied immediately, even while the container is running.
incus.nestingHint: Lets Docker or other containers run inside. The container stays unprivileged on this server.
incus.snapLead: A snapshot keeps everything inside as it is now. Rolling back to a snapshot loses everything that changed after it.
incus.snap.name: Name
incus.renameLead: The name is also the host name: the system inside gets it, and the computer in Hata and the backups are renamed too.
incus.renameLeadRunning: {name} is stopped briefly and started again: Incus can rename only a stopped one. The system inside gets the new host name, and the computer in Hata and the backups are renamed too.
incus.renameLeadVmStopped: The computer in Hata and the backups are renamed too. The system inside keeps its old host name until you change it there: the files of a stopped virtual machine cannot be reached.
incus.cloneLead: A copy of everything inside, without the snapshots; it is started as soon as it is ready. The clone gets its own address, machine ID and SSH keys.
incus.cloneLeadRunning: {name} keeps running: the clone is made from a snapshot taken now, without the older snapshots, and is started as soon as it is ready. It gets its own address, machine ID and SSH keys.
incus.cloneMachine: Hata's client in the clone connects as a new computer: the clone becomes a separate computer with the same apps.
error.containers.place.away: The disk of the storage {name} is not connected.
incus.removeLead: It will be stopped and deleted, together with its snapshots and everything inside it.
incus.removeLeadMachine: It will be stopped and deleted, together with its snapshots and everything inside it, including its apps and their data, and removed from the list of computers.
tools.incus.what: Makes system containers: separate Linux systems on this server.
tools.holds.containers: There are containers or virtual machines. Delete them first.

error.containers.noScreen: {name} is a container: it has a console, not a screen.
incus.vm.title: Virtual machines
incus.vm.lead: A virtual machine has a kernel of its own: for systems that need it, or where a container is not enough. It is a test feature of Hata for now.
incus.vm.limit.limits: A VM reserves all the memory it is given; a container needs less for the same work.
incus.vm.limit.images: Only systems tested as a virtual machine are offered: Debian, Ubuntu (also with a desktop), Fedora and Rocky Linux.
incus.vm.limit.screen: Its screen opens right in Hata, and a system can be installed from a disc image.
incus.vm.limit.space: The packages take about 400 MB more; a VM's disk is 10 GB unless you choose another size.
incus.vm.noArch: Virtual machines are offered on x86 servers only for now.
incus.vm.noKvm: Hardware virtualisation is not available (/dev/kvm is missing): it is switched off in the BIOS/UEFI, or this server is itself a virtual machine without nested virtualisation.
incus.vm.newLead: The system is downloaded once from the image server of Incus. The VM boots its own kernel, so it starts in about a minute.
incus.vm.note: Virtual machines are a test feature: on x86 servers only, from the systems listed here; Ubuntu with a desktop takes 4 GB of memory and 20 GB of disk.
incus.disc.title: Installation discs (ISO)
incus.disc.lead: System installers (.iso files) for a new virtual machine: it starts with the disc in its drive, and you install the system on its screen, as on any computer.
incus.disc.removeLead: The disc image is deleted from Incus. VMs installed from it are not affected.
incus.disc.ejected: Disc ejected from {name}: it now boots from its own disk
incus.disc.note: The VM starts with the disc in its drive and an empty disk; its screen opens and you install the system there. Hata's client is not installed automatically — once the system is installed, add it under Computers → Add… → Another computer, and eject the disc from the VM's menu.
incus.win.hint: TPM and Secure Boot are on; the disk is on NVMe and the disc on USB, so the installer sees both without drivers. The virtio drivers disc goes into a second drive: the network works once you run virtio-win-gt-x64.msi from it after installing Windows. Windows 11 requires 4 GB of memory and a 64 GB disk.
incus.win.hintNoDrivers: TPM and Secure Boot are on; the disk is on NVMe and the disc on USB, so the installer sees both without drivers. The network needs the virtio drivers: add “Drivers for Windows” under Disc images first, and they go into a second drive. Windows 11 requires 4 GB of memory and a 64 GB disk.
incus.win.driversHint: Fedora's virtio drivers disc (about 850 MB): Windows needs it for networking.
incus.disc.imageHint: Any system's installer: Hata does not know what is on the disc.
incus.disc.linkTitle: A disc image by a link
incus.disc.localTitle: A disc image from this computer
incus.disc.addLead: The image is saved straight into an Incus storage; no temporary copy is kept on the way.
incus.disc.urlHint: A link to an .iso file, as the system's site gives it.
incus.disc.noVms: Virtual machines are not set up on this server: see Computers → This server.
incus.vm.diskHint: Space is used only as the disk fills up.
tools.incus-vm.what: Runs Incus's virtual machines: QEMU, the firmware and the agent inside them.
tools.holds.vms: There are virtual machines. Delete them first.
tools.cannot.nested: Not available here: Hata itself runs in a container with a limited range of user IDs, and containers and virtual machines cannot be created inside one.
tools.cannot.noKvm: Not available here: hardware virtualisation is missing (disabled in BIOS/UEFI, or Hata itself runs in a virtual machine).
tools.cannot.noArch: Not available here: virtual machines are supported on x86 processors only.
error.containers.vm.noArch: Virtual machines are offered on x86 servers only for now.
error.containers.vm.noKvm: Hardware virtualisation is not available on this server (/dev/kvm is missing).
error.containers.vm.notInstalled: Install the virtual machine packages first.
error.containers.vm.notReady: The packages are installed, but Incus does not see QEMU after its restart.
error.containers.vm.noAgent: {name} started, but the agent inside did not answer within three minutes.
incus.vm.clientHint: The VM becomes one of the computers of Hata: its apps, files, terminal and backups.
incus.vm.limitsLead: The number of cores changes at once. The memory of a running virtual machine can be lowered at once, but raised above the amount it started with only after it is stopped.
backup.incus.title: Containers and virtual machines
backup.incus.lead: Each is backed up whole — its system and everything in it — and is stopped while the backup is taken. Incus first writes the export into /var/lib/incus, so free space for it is temporarily needed there too.
backup.incus.restoreLead: {name} is restored whole to its state at {time}: everything changed since then is lost, and so are its own snapshots. It reconnects to Hata by itself.
incus.place.title: Storage
incus.place.lead: Folders the containers and virtual machines are kept in. A storage on btrfs lets a container's disk be limited.
incus.place.whereHint: On the system disk unless you choose a folder on another one. The folder must be empty or not there yet; not the data folder or the backups.
incus.place.awayHint: Incus cannot reach this folder: the disk it is on is not connected. What is kept here starts by itself once the disk is back.
incus.place.label: Storage
incus.place.moveLead: It is copied whole, with its snapshots, and removed from the old storage.
incus.place.moveLeadRunning: It is stopped, copied whole with its snapshots, removed from the old storage and started again.
incus.bad.place: Choose a storage from the list.
error.containers.place.system: A system folder cannot be used.
error.containers.place.state: Hata's own folder cannot be used.
error.containers.place.data: The data folder cannot be used: it is mounted into apps and shared.
error.containers.place.backups: The backup folder cannot be used.
error.containers.place.taken: This folder is another storage, or lies inside or around one.
error.containers.place.fs: This folder is on a file system that cannot hold containers: FAT, exFAT and NTFS keep no owners of files, and network or merged folders do not fit either. Choose a folder on a disk with ext4, btrfs or XFS; a disk is formatted in Storage → Disks.
error.containers.place.notEmpty: {path} is not empty: choose an empty folder or a new one.
error.containers.place.isStandard: {name} is the default storage: make another one the default first.
error.containers.place.inUse: {name} still holds containers or VMs: {n}. Move them first.
error.disk.holds.containers: Containers are kept here. Move them to another storage first.
activity.containers.screen: Screen of a virtual machine opened: {target}
error.containers.place.profile: Incus's default profile keeps its disk in {name}: this storage cannot be taken away.
incus.diskLimitHint: Empty — as much as the storage has.
incus.diskNotHere: {place} is a plain folder, so a container's disk size cannot be limited there. A storage on btrfs can do it — move the container there to limit its disk.
incus.vm.diskGrow: Can only be increased: a smaller disk would cut off part of the system inside. A running VM gets the new size after a restart.
incus.bad.diskShrink: A virtual machine's disk can only be increased.
error.containers.disk.notHere: {name} is a plain folder, so a container's disk size cannot be limited there. Choose a storage on btrfs.
